templates.pattern: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Calculate the distance travelled by light in [T] seconds.
templates.explanation:
Distance = speed × time
= 3 × 10⁸ × [T]
= [RESULT] m

The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s. At GCSE level we use 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Light from the Sun takes approximately 8 minutes to reach Earth.

templates.pattern: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of [A] degrees. Calculate the angle of reflection in degrees.
templates.explanation:
Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
= [A] degrees
= [RESULT] degrees

Both angles are always measured from the normal to the surface — not from the surface itself. This law applies to all types of reflection.

templates.pattern: An object is placed [U] cm in front of a plane mirror. Calculate the distance of the image behind the mirror in cm.
templates.explanation:
In a plane mirror the image is always formed as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Image distance = object distance = [RESULT] cm

The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright and laterally inverted. It cannot be projected onto a screen.

templates.pattern: A glass block has a refractive index of [N]. The speed of light in a vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the speed of light inside the glass block in m/s.
templates.explanation:
Speed of light in medium = c ÷ n
= 3 × 10⁸ ÷ [N]
= [RESULT] m/s

The refractive index tells us how much slower light travels in a medium compared to a vacuum. A higher refractive index means slower light.

templates.pattern: A concave mirror has a focal length of [F] cm. Calculate the radius of curvature of the mirror in cm.
templates.explanation:
Radius of curvature = 2 × focal length
= 2 × [F]
= [RESULT] cm

The centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere of which the mirror forms a part. The focal point lies exactly halfway between the mirror and the centre of curvature.

templates.pattern: A spherical mirror has a radius of curvature of [R] cm. Calculate the focal length of the mirror in cm.
templates.explanation:
Focal length = radius of curvature ÷ 2
= [R] ÷ 2
= [RESULT] cm

This relationship holds for both concave and convex mirrors. The focal length is always half the radius of curvature.

templates.pattern: A ray of light hits a surface at [A] degrees measured from the surface itself. Calculate the angle of incidence measured from the normal in degrees.
templates.explanation:
Angle from normal = 90° − angle from surface
= 90 − [A]
= [RESULT] degrees

In optics all angles are always measured from the normal — the imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence. This is a very common source of error for students.

templates.pattern: A converging lens has a focal length of [F] cm. An object is placed [U] cm from the lens. Calculate the image distance in cm.
templates.explanation:
Lens formula: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u
Rearranging: v = uF ÷ (u − f)
= [U] × [F] ÷ ([U] − [F])
= [U*F] ÷ [U-F]
= [RESULT] cm

A positive image distance means the image is real and on the opposite side of the lens from the object.

templates.pattern: A lens produces an image [V] cm from the lens. The object is placed [U] cm from the lens. Calculate the magnification produced by the lens.
templates.explanation:
Magnification = image distance ÷ object distance
= v ÷ u
= [V] ÷ [U]
= [RESULT]

A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object. A magnification less than 1 means the image is smaller. A negative value means the image is inverted.

templates.pattern: An object is [H] cm tall. A lens produces a magnification of [M]. Calculate the height of the image in cm.
templates.explanation:
Image height = object height × magnification
= [H] × [M]
= [RESULT] cm

Magnification tells us how many times larger the image is compared to the object. A magnification of [M] means the image is [M] times the size of the object.
